analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to get your permission before sharing your financial data with their affiliates.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a vote; its only action after referral was a repeat of the sponsor's remarks seven months later.
analysis.plain_summary: Congress passed the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act in 1999, which let banks share customers' personal financial information with affiliated companies unless the customer said no. This bill would have flipped that: banks could not share your information with affiliates without your permission, would be barred from selling or sharing detailed records of your spending, could not use your health information when deciding whether to lend to you, could not share your account numbers, and state attorneys general could sue to enforce these rules. It was introduced in May 2000, referred to the Banking Committee, and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Any consumer with a bank account, credit card, or loan. Today, under the law as it stands, your bank can share your financial details with companies in its corporate family — insurance arms, investment arms, marketing companies — unless you actively opt out. This bill would have required the bank to get your yes first, and would have banned outright the transfer of your individual transaction histories, your account numbers, and the use of your health information in credit decisions.

how_it_helps.text: Reverses the default in the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act so that sharing customer information with affiliates — not just outside companies — requires the customer's consent first [S2][S3].

Bans banks from transferring individualized lists of a customer's transactions, interests, or preferences (derived from check, debit, or credit card activity) unless the customer affirmatively consents, and bars transfers of aggregate lists built from individually identifiable health information [S2][S3].

Prohibits a financial institution from using individually identifiable health information obtained from affiliates or third parties when deciding whether or on what terms to offer credit, unless the customer consents and the same information is required of all applicants [S2][S3].

Bars disclosure of a customer's account number or comparable access code to affiliates as well as nonaffiliated third parties, and requires privacy notices before a customer relationship is established rather than when it is established [S2][S3].

Gives consumers the right to see and correct the information a financial institution holds about them, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents to enforce the privacy rules and obtain damages [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, insurers, and securities firms that had planned to pool customer data across their corporate families under the 1999 law, plus direct marketers who buy customer lists. Complying would mean building consent systems, restricting data flows, and forgoing revenue from sharing and selling customer information. Some compliance costs could be passed to customers through fees.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is costly: financial institutions of every size, including community banks and credit unions, would have to build systems for consent, access requests, and corrections, and those costs are likely to show up in fees or reduced free services [S3].

The bill itself allows financial institutions to charge customers a reasonable fee for access to their own information, and exempts from the access right things like the algorithms used to derive credit scores, limiting how much transparency customers would actually get [S3].

It preserves broad exceptions: banks could still share information to market their own products to their own customers, and to run consolidated call centers and statements, so a meaningful amount of affiliate data-sharing would continue without consent [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary customers the gains are substantial and the costs are modest: the information at stake — transaction histories, account numbers, health details — is exactly the kind that can be used to target, price, or deny financial products. The main honest cost falls on regulated firms, and the bill's own exceptions leave some data-sharing channels open. On balance it is a pro-consumer bill whose main casualties are banks' data-sharing plans.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee from May 2000 until the Congress ended in January 2001; the committee never held a markup, never reported it, and the Senate never voted on it.

narrative.text: Leahy introduced the bill with nine Democratic cosponsors on May 4, 2000, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S4][S5].
The bill's only further action was a repeat of the sponsor's introductory remarks on December 14, 2000; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S5].
The 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other financial firms kept the rights the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act gave them — to share customer data across affiliates and sell lists unless customers opt out — with no new consent requirements or enforcement.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks in May and again in December 2000.

for.name: Sens. Sarbanes, Robb, Dodd, Kerry, Bryan, Edwards, Durbin, Harkin, and Feinstein

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Phil Gramm (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; it received no action beyond referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Banks, insurers, and securities firms operating under the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
against.what_they_did: Opposed affiliate-sharing and health-information restrictions of this kind, having won the affiliate-sharing right in the 1999 law; the committee chaired by its leading Senate defender never acted on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were Democrats; the Republican-majority Banking Committee never took the bill up, and there was no Republican cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have taken away their ability to freely share customers' financial data with affiliates and would have banned sharing transaction histories and account numbers. The 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act had handed them this data-sharing right; the industry's gain comes at the cost of customers' control over their own information.

The bill would have cut off the flow of individualized customer lists — spending habits, interests, preferences — and lists built from health information, a supply these firms buy from financial institutions.
